summaries.example: Imagine describing a cat in layers: first, “This is a body,” then “This body is alive,” then “This animal is a cat,” and finally “This cat is black.” Some medieval philosophers thought these layers showed different forms inside the thing. Other philosophers thought the words were simply different ways of describing one basic thing.
summaries.summary: “Binarium famosissimum” is a modern name for two theories discussed by medieval philosophers: universal hylomorphism and plurality of forms. Universal hylomorphism says that every created thing is made from matter and form. This includes things that do not seem physical, such as angels or a human soul after death, because the theory allows a special kind of “spiritual matter.” God alone is completely simple. Plurality of forms says that one physical thing may contain several substantial forms, not merely many ordinary qualities like color or size. Thinkers disagreed about how many forms a human body or another thing has. Many authors held both theories, while Thomas Aquinas rejected both in their usual versions. The entry also explains that the two ideas may fit together because some philosophers thought the layers in true statements reveal layers in reality. Still, the phrase for this pair seems to be a much later historical label, and the connection between the theories was not accepted by every thinker.
key_ideas: “Binarium famosissimum” means “most famous pair.” Modern historians used it for universal hylomorphism and plurality of forms.
Many medieval thinkers held both doctrines, but others, including Thomas Aquinas, rejected one or both.
The pairing was probably created by twentieth-century scholars, not used as a name for this pair by medieval thinkers.
The theories can be connected to a question about whether the layers in our true descriptions match real parts in things.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic shows how philosophers investigate what things are made of and how language connects to reality. It also teaches an important lesson about history: a label used by modern scholars may not have been used by the people being studied. Studying disagreements between medieval thinkers helps us see that philosophical traditions are not all of one kind.

important_terms.definition: A medieval idea that every created thing is made from matter and form. In this view, only God is completely simple, and even spiritual creatures have a kind of matter.
The idea that one physical thing can have several substantial forms, or deep features that help make it the kind of thing it is.
A technical word meaning “made of parts” or “put together.” Medieval thinkers used it when discussing created things.
A feature that helps make something what it is, rather than merely describing an extra quality such as color.

questions_to_think_about: When we describe something in several ways, are we finding real layers in it or just using different words?
Why might a philosopher think that only God can be completely simple?
Could a thing have several deep forms and still be one thing?
Why should historians be careful when giving an old idea a new name?

summaries.example: Consider the sequence “This is a body,” “This body is alive,” “This organism is an animal,” and “This animal is a cat.” A universal hylomorphist might treat each level as adding a form to an increasingly determinate underlying subject, producing a layered metaphysical structure. A Thomistic alternative says that the sequence need not reveal several substantial components: the same individual may have one substantial form, while “body,” “organism,” “animal,” and “cat” describe it at different levels. The predicate “black,” by contrast, introduces an accidental feature.
summaries.summary: The entry examines a pair of doctrines that twentieth-century historians called the “binarium famosissimum,” or “most famous pair”: universal hylomorphism and plurality of forms. Universal hylomorphism holds that every created substance is composed of matter and form, whereas God is metaphysically simple. Since angels and the human soul after death are not ordinary physical objects, proponents distinguished corporeal matter from spiritual matter. The doctrine may be supported by the thought that whatever is caused is composite and that God, as first cause, must therefore be simple, although the entry notes that medieval authors do not clearly state this full argument. Plurality of forms claims that a material substance has several substantial forms. It should not be confused with the less controversial claim that a substance has numerous accidental properties. The theories often appeared together, but their relationship is not historically straightforward. One possible link is a view of predication according to which the structure of true statements mirrors the structure of reality: “body,” “living thing,” “animal,” and “cat” would correspond to successive forms. An Aristotelian or Thomistic alternative denies that ordinary predication maps reality so directly. Aquinas instead explains created composition through essence and existence and rejects a plurality of substantial forms. The entry concludes that the pairing is mainly a later scholarly construction, even though some medieval thinkers held both doctrines.
key_ideas: The “most famous pair” consists of universal hylomorphism and plurality of forms, doctrines often associated with some Augustinian scholastics of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries.
Universal hylomorphism argues that all creatures are composite, including angels and separated souls, by allowing a distinction between corporeal and spiritual matter.
Plurality of forms concerns multiple substantial forms in one substance, not merely the many accidental properties everyone accepted.
Aquinas rejected universal hylomorphism while explaining creaturely composition through essence and existence; he also rejected multiple substantial forms in one substance.
The modern pairing may reflect a shared theory of predication: layers in true descriptions were taken to correspond to layers in reality.
The historical label is probably a twentieth-century construction, so the connection should not be projected uncritically onto medieval authors.
summaries.why_it_matters: The issue matters for metaphysics because it asks whether reality is layered into matter and forms, how a thing remains one thing, and whether language reveals its structure. It also matters for intellectual history. Medieval authors held varied positions, and the later label “binarium famosissimum” can make their disagreements look more unified than the evidence warrants. Careful historical analysis separates what thinkers actually argued from patterns identified by later scholars.

important_terms.definition: The view that every created substance is composed of matter and form, while God alone is absolutely simple. It extends matter-form composition beyond ordinary physical objects to spiritual substances.
The theory that a single material substance contains more than one substantial form. It is stronger than the uncontroversial claim that things have many accidental qualities.
A composition in which an underlying, relatively indeterminate factor is organized or determined by form. In medieval discussions, this is the basic matter-form structure.
A feature that helps constitute a thing as the kind of substance it is. It differs from an accidental form, such as a color or other changeable quality.
A nonessential feature that can belong to a substance without making it the kind of thing it is, such as being black in the example of a cat.
The condition of having no metaphysical parts or composition. The entry reports that universal hylomorphism assigns absolute simplicity uniquely to God.
The philosophical act of saying something about a subject, such as saying that a cat is black or that it is an animal.
The medieval school of thought associated in this entry with thinkers who opposed the two doctrines, especially Thomas Aquinas, although the historical divisions were complex.

questions_to_think_about: Does a sequence of increasingly specific descriptions show increasingly deep metaphysical parts, or can one thing simply be described at different levels?
What argument might connect creation and the claim that every created thing is composite?
Why is plurality of substantial forms a stronger position than saying that a thing has many qualities?
How does the distinction between essence and existence offer Aquinas an alternative to universal hylomorphism?
What can the later history of the phrase “binarium famosissimum” teach us about interpreting historical categories?

summaries.example: Suppose your class describes a tree: “It is a body,” “It is alive,” “It is a plant,” and “It is an oak.” One philosopher might say that each step points to a deeper form added to an underlying material basis. Another might say that these are increasingly specific descriptions of one substance, not proof that the tree has several substantial forms. Saying “the oak is green” would add a different kind of feature: an accidental form, because the tree could lose its color without ceasing to be an oak.
summaries.summary: “Binarium famosissimum” is a phrase used by modern historians for two medieval doctrines: universal hylomorphism and plurality of forms. The first says that every created substance is composed of matter and form. God is the exception because God alone is absolutely simple. Since angels and the human soul after death are not ordinary physical bodies, supporters of the theory spoke of “spiritual matter” as well as bodily matter. The second doctrine says that one material substance can have more than one substantial form. This is different from saying that a thing has many accidental features, such as color or size. Medieval thinkers disagreed about how many substantial forms a human being or other body might have. Several authors held both theories, while Thomas Aquinas rejected them. Aquinas maintained that creatures are composed through essence and existence, whether or not they also have matter and form. He also argued that only the first form entering a substance could be substantial; later forms would be accidental. The entry explores why the two doctrines have often been linked. A philosopher might believe that the order of true descriptions—body, living thing, animal, cat—matches layers in reality. Other philosophers, following an Aristotelian or Thomistic approach, denied that language gives such a direct map of metaphysical structure. Finally, the phrase itself seems to be a twentieth-century scholarly invention rather than a medieval name for the pair.
key_ideas: The phrase “binarium famosissimum” is a later name for two doctrines often connected with some medieval Augustinian thinkers.
Universal hylomorphism says that creatures are made of matter and form, even when they are not ordinary physical objects.
Plurality of forms says that one material substance can have several substantial forms, not merely several qualities.
Thomas Aquinas rejected universal hylomorphism and argued that creatures can be composite through essence and existence instead.
Scholars connect the theories because both can fit the idea that true descriptions reveal real layers in things.
The medieval evidence does not show that thinkers themselves treated these doctrines as one named pair.
summaries.why_it_matters: This debate helps explain different answers to a basic philosophical question: what makes a thing the thing it is? It also shows how views about language, matter, and form can support one another. Historically, it reminds us to distinguish medieval doctrines from the categories later historians use to organize them.

important_terms.definition: The view that all created substances contain matter and form, including spiritual beings in a special sense. God alone is completely without metaphysical composition.
The view that a single material substance has several substantial forms, such as a basic bodily form plus other forms connected with living or sensing.
Something made up of parts or principles rather than being completely simple.
A deep organizing principle that helps make a substance the kind of thing it is.
A feature that belongs to a thing but is not required for it to remain that kind of thing, such as a color.
Saying something about something else, as when we say that a tree is alive or that it is green.
A school or approach linked in the entry with thinkers such as Thomas Aquinas, who criticized both doctrines in their standard forms.

questions_to_think_about: If a tree can be described as a body, plant, and oak, does that mean it has several forms?
Why might someone think that angels or souls need a special kind of matter?
What is the difference between a substantial form and an accidental form?
Why did Aquinas think matter and form were not needed to explain every creature’s composition?
How can a modern label change the way we understand an older philosophical debate?
